newsitem.title: GERMANY: Senior European figures seek credible euro.
newsitem.headline: Senior European figures seek credible euro.

text.p: Leading European bankers and politicians on Thursday night stepped up calls for a stable single European currency, but said countries seeking to join first needed to prove their long-term financial health.

Speaking on German television, the president of Germany's powerful Bundesbank, Hans Tietmeyer, said sustainability, not precise figures, was of primary importance for the success of the single currency, which is due to start on January 1, 1999.
"It's not a question of whether a country meets a particular figure on a particular date, it is a question of the long-term sustainability of the euro," he said.

In a separate television interview, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who has been at loggerheads with Tietmeyer in recent weeks over Bonn's attempts to revalue Germany's reserves, agreed that credibility was what counted when it came to European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Waigel said he was not willing to engage in a debate about decimal points in Maastricht criteria for EMU.

"I will not engage in a discussion about decimal points. It is a question of credibility," Waigel said, referring to the EMU entry criterion that member states should reduce budget deficits to at most three percent of GDP in 1997.
"If Germany were to discuss figures like 3.3 or 3.2 percent, others would start to talk about 3.8 percent," Waigel said.
He also said that the German government would be taking measures in the 1997 budget to reach the 3.0 percent target.
The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) released a report earlier on Thursday which forecast that Germany's deficit would be 3.2 percent of GDP this year.
But Waigel, who has come in for sharp criticism in recent weeks for failing to present credible plans to ensure Germany meets Maastricht entry rules, said that Germany would beat the OECD's forecast.
"We will do better than 3.2 percent," he said.

Separately, Gerhard Schroeder, a leading figure in Germany's opposition Social Democrats, said that would-be euro members must closely adhere to the criteria for EMU to ensure the trust of the financial markets.

"If the criteria are not held to, then people will not believe in the euro, and the financial markets will not believe in the euro," Schroeder said, adding that if the criteria were not held to, higher interest rates could result.
The outgoing President of the European Monetary Institute (EMI), Alexandre Lamfalussy, said the stability of monetary union would depend on the monetary policy of the future European Central Bank.
"I am convinced that the ECB will be in a position to follow a stability-oriented monetary policy," Lamfalussy said.
A key issue in the stability debate concerns attempts by countries such as Italy and Spain to join EMU.

Some bankers and politicians, including Waigel himself at one point, have gone on record as saying that allowing such countries to join was not an option as they were unlikely to meet the criteria and could lead to a softer euro.

Tietmeyer said that he was not opposed to Italy joining EMU. "No, quite the opposite," he said. "Every country has the same chance (to join EMU)," he said. "Italy has the same chance as every other country."
